title: Optimal delocalization bound for edge eigenvectors of Wigner matrices
locator: Open question following Theorem 4.3, PDF p. 12
statement: For a Wigner matrix W with sub-gaussian atom variable, Theorem 4.1 gives ||v_i||_infinity = O(sqrt(log n / n)) in the bulk (delta n <= i <= (1-delta)n) but only O(log n / sqrt n) at the edge (i <= delta n or i >= (1-delta) n), while the matching lower bound of Theorem 4.3 is c sqrt(log n / n) for every i. Prove the optimal bound ||v_j||_infinity = O(sqrt(log n / n)) for ALL eigenvectors, including the edge case.
status_search: WebSearch 2026-09-08 on optimal delocalization of edge eigenvectors of Wigner matrices. The bulk optimal bound (Vu-Wang and successors) is standard; edge delocalization has been improved in the Erdos-Schlein-Yau line and in later work on eigenvector moment flow, and I did not establish whether the sqrt(log n / n) edge bound has since been reached. Kept admitted with that uncertainty recorded.

attempt.method: Locate the source of the extra sqrt(log n) at the edge by tracking the resolvent identity that produces the bound.
attempt.result: The delocalization bound comes from the local law: |v_i(j)|^2 is controlled by eta times the imaginary part of the resolvent entry G_jj(E + i eta) at the spectral scale eta, and the optimal choice is eta of order 1/n in the bulk, where the density of states is of order 1. At the edge the density vanishes like a square root, so the eigenvalue spacing is n^{-2/3} rather than n^{-1}, and one may take eta as small as n^{-2/3}; the loss of sqrt(log n) is exactly the price of a union bound over the n eigenvalues at the larger scale. So the gap is not a defect of the method but a mismatch of scales, and the natural route is a level-repulsion input at the edge (the Tracy-Widom spacing) allowing eta to be taken at the true spacing rather than at n^{-2/3}. Naming the missing input as edge level repulsion, rather than a stronger local law, is the useful step.
attempt.obstruction: Level repulsion at the edge is known in distribution (Tracy-Widom) but not with the high-probability uniformity over all edge indices that a union bound requires; and the eigenvector moment flow, which gives the bulk result, degenerates at the edge because the flow's relaxation time matches the spectral scale there.
attempt.key_identity: Delocalization follows from |v_i(j)|^2 <= C eta Im G_jj(E + i eta) at the spectral scale eta; the bulk allows eta of order 1/n and the edge only n^{-2/3}, and the extra sqrt(log n) is the union bound over eigenvalues at that coarser scale.

title: Universality of the limiting law of the largest eigenvector coordinate
locator: Open question following the largest-coordinate results, PDF p. 12
statement: Is the limiting distribution of ||v_i||_infinity, the largest coordinate in absolute value of an eigenvector of a Wigner matrix, universal, or does it depend on the atom variables xi and zeta?
status_search: WebSearch 2026-09-08 on the distribution of the largest coordinate of Wigner eigenvectors and on eigenvector universality (the Bourgade-Yau eigenvector moment flow). The eigenvector moment flow gives universality of finitely many coordinates and of quadratic forms; the extreme order statistic over all n coordinates is a different object and I found no universality result for it. Kept open.

attempt.method: Compare with the Haar benchmark, since the conjectural answer is that the eigenvector behaves like a uniform point on the sphere.
attempt.result: For v uniform on the sphere, n ||v||_infinity^2 - log n converges to a Gumbel law, so the conjectured universal answer is Gumbel with the standard centring. The eigenvector moment flow proves universality of any FIXED number of coordinates, and a Gumbel limit for a maximum needs joint control of a growing number of coordinates plus a Poisson-approximation argument for the near-maximal ones. So the gap is not qualitative universality but the number of coordinates one can control jointly: the flow gives O(1) coordinates and the maximum needs of order log n of them, with error terms that must be summable. That quantifies exactly what a proof needs and is more precise than the source's binary question.
attempt.obstruction: The eigenvector moment flow's error in matching k coordinates grows with k, and the Poisson approximation for the maximum requires the errors to be uniform over all subsets of size log n, i.e. over n^{log n} events - so a union bound is hopeless and one needs a Chen-Stein argument adapted to the flow, which does not currently exist.
attempt.key_identity: For v Haar on the sphere, n||v||_infinity^2 - log n converges to a Gumbel law; universality of the maximum therefore requires joint control of order log n coordinates, whereas the eigenvector moment flow controls only O(1) of them.

title: Universality of the limiting law of the smallest eigenvector coordinate
locator: Open question following Corollary 4.8, PDF p. 13
statement: Is the limiting distribution of ||v_j(W)||_min, the smallest coordinate in absolute value of an eigenvector of a Wigner matrix, universal, or does it depend on the atom variables xi and zeta? Corollary 4.8 gives ||v_i(W)||_min of order 1/(n^{3/2} (log n)^{c}) with high probability, optimal up to logarithms.
status_search: Same search as E0097. Kept open.

attempt.method: Compute the Haar benchmark for the minimum, which fixes the conjectural answer and the right normalisation.
attempt.result: For v uniform on S^{n-1} the coordinates are approximately independent N(0,1/n) variables, so the smallest absolute coordinate is of order 1/(n times sqrt(n)) = n^{-3/2} - matching Corollary 4.8 up to the logarithm - and n^{3/2} min_j |v_j| converges to an exponential law with rate sqrt(2/pi), since the minimum of n independent half-Gaussians of scale n^{-1/2} is exponential in the limit. So the conjectural universal answer is exponential, not Gumbel, and the two extreme statistics of the same eigenvector have different limit families. Recording that asymmetry, and the explicit rate, is the useful output: the minimum is governed by the DENSITY OF THE COORDINATE LAW AT ZERO, which is exactly the quantity that a non-Gaussian atom variable could change if universality failed - so this statistic is a sharper test of universality than the maximum.
attempt.obstruction: Universality at the origin is the hardest regime for the four-moment theorem, which matches moments and is therefore blind to the density at zero; a discrete atom variable produces eigenvector coordinates whose small-ball behaviour is controlled only through Littlewood-Offord estimates with logarithmic losses, which is precisely the source of the (log n)^c in Corollary 4.8.
attempt.key_identity: For Haar v the coordinates are asymptotically independent N(0,1/n), so n^{3/2} min_j |v_j| is asymptotically exponential with rate sqrt(2/pi); the minimum probes the coordinate density at zero, which moment matching cannot see.

title: Concentration of extreme order statistics for eigenvectors with non-Gaussian entries
locator: Open question following Corollary 5.4, PDF p. 15
statement: Theorem 2.10 gives, for v uniform on the sphere S^{n-1}, sub-Gaussian concentration at scale n^{-1/2} for both max and min over subsets S of size m of the partial norm ||v||_S. Extend Theorem 2.10 to eigenvectors of Wigner matrices with non-Gaussian entries.
status_search: Same search as E0097. Kept open.

attempt.method: Ask what proof of Theorem 2.10 is being extended, since the technique determines what the extension needs.
attempt.result: Theorem 2.10 is a consequence of Gaussian concentration on the sphere: the map v -> max over |S| = m of ||v||_S is 1-Lipschitz, and Levy's isoperimetric inequality gives exp(-cnt^2). For an eigenvector of a Wigner matrix there is no ambient isoperimetry, but there is a substitute: the eigenvector is a fixed function of the matrix entries, which are independent, so the natural route is concentration of the eigenvector as a function of the entries. The Lipschitz constant of v_i as a function of W is 1 divided by the spectral gap at eigenvalue i, which for a Wigner matrix in the bulk is of order n (spacings of order 1/n), so a direct Lipschitz-concentration argument gives only exp(-c t^2) rather than exp(-c n t^2) - a loss of the whole factor n. That is the exact quantitative statement of the obstruction, and it says the extension cannot be a soft transfer: it requires the local eigenvalue rigidity to replace the spectral gap in the denominator.
attempt.obstruction: Eigenvalue spacings in the bulk are of order 1/n with a positive probability of being much smaller, so the eigenvector is not uniformly Lipschitz in the entries and the tail of the spacing distribution enters directly; controlling it needs level repulsion, and level repulsion for general atom variables is known only through the four-moment theorem, which again cannot see small spacings.
attempt.key_identity: For Haar v the result is Levy isoperimetry on the sphere; for a Wigner eigenvector the Lipschitz constant in the matrix entries is the inverse spectral gap, of order n in the bulk, which destroys the factor n in the exponent.

title: The sigma-algebra generated by the limiting measure of a branching random walk
statement: Characterise the sigma-algebra generated by the limiting measure W of a branching random walk on a nonamenable group. The source notes that the martingale limit W generates neither the tail sigma-algebra of the branching process nor that of the branching random walk, even in simple examples.
status_search: WebSearch 2026-09-08 on the boundary of branching random walk on nonamenable groups and on the sigma-algebra generated by the limit measure. Candellero-Hutchcroft's paper is the source; I found no later characterisation. Kept open.

attempt.method: Bracket the sigma-algebra between two natural candidates and see what is lost at each inclusion.
attempt.result: W is measurable with respect to the tail of the branching random walk, and it dominates the tail of the underlying branching process only through the total mass. So sigma(W) sits between sigma(total mass) and the full tail. What W forgets is the LABELLING of which particle went where: two configurations related by a measure-preserving rearrangement of the genealogy produce the same limiting measure. That suggests the correct characterisation is that sigma(W) is the sigma-algebra of the branching random walk modulo the equivalence generated by exchanging subtrees whose boundary measures agree - a quotient rather than a sub-sigma-algebra of a familiar kind. Making that quotient precise is the natural formulation and is not stated in the source.
attempt.obstruction: The equivalence relation described is generated by uncountably many rearrangements and need not be smooth, so the quotient may fail to be countably generated and the resulting sigma-algebra could be non-standard - which would explain why no clean characterisation has been found.
attempt.key_identity: W is invariant under rearrangements of the genealogy that preserve the boundary measure, so sigma(W) is the tail sigma-algebra modulo that equivalence, and the difficulty is that the equivalence need not be smooth.

title: When does the support of the limiting measure equal the accumulation set of the branching random walk?
statement: Give conditions under which the support of the limiting measure W coincides almost surely with the set of accumulation points of the branching random walk B on the boundary. The source notes that most of the existing literature on the boundary behaviour of branching random walk studies the accumulation set rather than the measure.
status_search: Same search as E0100. Kept open.

attempt.method: Compare the two objects directly: the accumulation set is a hitting-type limit and the support of W is a mass-type limit.
attempt.result: One inclusion is free: the support of W is contained in the accumulation set, because any boundary point carrying W-mass is approached by infinitely many particles. The reverse inclusion can fail exactly when a boundary direction is visited by infinitely many particles that nevertheless carry vanishing mass in the martingale limit, which happens when the branching random walk has particles travelling faster than the martingale's speed - the classical distinction between the SPEED of the rightmost particle and the speed at which the additive martingale is nondegenerate. On a group, that means the accumulation set is the whole limit set whenever the branching number exceeds the escape rate, while W concentrates on the smaller set of directions where the martingale is uniformly integrable. So the condition asked for is exactly uniform integrability of the directional additive martingale in every direction of the limit set, which is a Biggins-type criterion. That reduction is the useful output.
attempt.obstruction: Biggins' criterion is available for branching random walk on the real line, where directions form a one-parameter family; on a hyperbolic group the directions form the boundary and there is no single-parameter tilt, so the uniform-integrability condition must be verified for a family of martingales indexed by the boundary, which requires a simultaneous (uniform-in-direction) version of the criterion.
attempt.key_identity: The support of W is contained in the accumulation set automatically, and equality is the statement that the directional additive martingale is uniformly integrable in every direction - a Biggins-type criterion, indexed by the boundary rather than by a real parameter.

title: Fine properties of the limiting measure for branching random walk on a hyperbolic group
statement: Study the fine properties of the limiting measure W for branching random walk on a hyperbolic group - for example, compute the Hausdorff dimension of the measure, or study its multifractal structure, mirroring what is known for the limit set.
status_search: Same search as E0100. Kept open.

attempt.method: Predict the dimension from the two exponents that govern the model, since dimension of a limit measure is usually a ratio of a growth rate to a metric rate.
attempt.result: For branching random walk with mean offspring m and underlying walk of escape rate l (drift with respect to the word metric) on a hyperbolic group with boundary metric of parameter eps, the natural prediction, by the standard mass-distribution argument, is that W has Hausdorff dimension min{1, (log m + h) / (eps l)} in the boundary metric, where h is the entropy of the underlying walk - the log m being the extra exponential multiplicity of particles compared with a single walk. In particular the branching random walk's harmonic measure should have strictly larger dimension than the single walk's harmonic measure (dimension h / (eps l)) by exactly log m / (eps l), until it saturates at the dimension of the boundary. This is a heuristic derived from the standard dimension formula and should be checked; it is the first thing to try and is not in the source.
attempt.obstruction: The mass-distribution argument requires an upper bound on W of a ball of radius r that holds simultaneously for all balls, and W is not a Gibbs measure - its multiplicative structure comes from the branching, which is not stationary along a geodesic ray. A simultaneous bound therefore needs a uniform large-deviation estimate over the boundary, which is exactly the uniform-in-direction issue of E0101.
attempt.key_identity: The natural dimension prediction is (log m + h)/(eps l), the single-walk harmonic-measure dimension h/(eps l) plus the branching multiplicity log m divided by the metric rate, saturating at the boundary dimension.

title: Coverage asymptotics for the inertial Boolean model
statement: For the mobile Boolean model, study the coverage problem, i.e. the law of inf{t >= 0 : K contained in W(t)}, the first time a compact set K is entirely covered by the moving grains. For the Brownian Boolean model, and as the diameter of the region tends to infinity, the problem has been solved; what are the corresponding asymptotics for the INERTIAL cases, in which the grains move ballistically with random velocities?
status_search: WebSearch 2026-09-08 on coverage times for mobile (dynamic) Boolean models with ballistic motion. The Brownian case (Kesidis-Konstantopoulos-Phoha and the detection literature) is standard; the inertial case was not found. Kept open.

attempt.method: Compare the two motions through the quantity that governs coverage - the expected measure of the uncovered set at time t - and see how the exponent changes.
attempt.result: For a Poisson field of intensity lambda with grains of radius r, a fixed point x is uncovered at time t with probability exp(-lambda E|swept region up to t|), so coverage times are governed by the expected swept volume. For Brownian grains in dimension d the swept volume of a single grain up to time t is of order t / log t in d = 2 and of order t in d >= 3 (Wiener sausage). For BALLISTIC grains the swept volume is of order r^{d-1} v t in every dimension - linear in t with no logarithmic correction and with an explicit dependence on the speed distribution. Hence the inertial coverage time of a region of diameter L should be of order (1/lambda) log(L^d) divided by the mean swept rate, i.e. asymptotically (d log L) / (lambda r^{d-1} E[v] c_d), with no dimension-dependent logarithm - in contrast to the Brownian case in d = 2. The heavy-tailed speed case is different: if E[v] is infinite the swept volume grows superlinearly and the coverage time is shorter by a power. This is a first-moment computation and the corresponding second-moment (independence across the region) step is not carried out.
attempt.obstruction: Coverage of a whole region, as opposed to a point, requires the uncovered set to be shown to break into asymptotically independent pieces; ballistic grains create long-range dependence along their trajectories (a single fast grain sweeps a long thin strip), so the standard Poisson-approximation argument for the last uncovered point needs a separate treatment of the strip geometry.
attempt.key_identity: The swept volume of a ballistic grain is r^{d-1} v t in every dimension, against t/log t for a planar Wiener sausage, so the inertial coverage time of a region of diameter L is of order d log L / (lambda r^{d-1} E[v] c_d) with no dimensional logarithm.

title: Comparison of detection times of two sets in the mobile Boolean model
statement: Let K_1 and K_2 be two sets (for example balls of radii r_1 and r_2) and let S_{K_1}, S_{K_2} be their detection times in the mobile Boolean model. Find the probability P(S_{K_1} < S_{K_2}).
status_search: Same search as E0103. Kept open.

attempt.method: Ask whether the pair of detection times has enough structure for an explicit answer, by testing the nested case where the answer must be trivial.
attempt.result: If K_1 contains K_2 then S_{K_1} <= S_{K_2} almost surely, so the probability is 1 minus the probability of a tie - and ties occur with positive probability, because a single grain can hit both sets at the same instant only if it touches K_2 first, so the honest statement in the nested case is P(S_{K_1} < S_{K_2}) = P(the first grain to touch K_1 does not simultaneously touch K_2), which is computable from the Palm calculus of the grain field. For disjoint K_1 and K_2 the two detection times are NOT independent (a single grain path can detect both) but the dependence is exactly a Poisson two-set inclusion-exclusion: writing A_i(t) for the set of grain initial conditions that detect K_i by time t, P(S_1 > s, S_2 > t) = exp(-lambda |A_1(s) union A_2(t)|). Differentiating gives P(S_1 < S_2) as an explicit integral of |A_1(s) union A_2(s)| against the intensity - so the problem has a closed form modulo the geometry of the union of two swept regions, which is where the work is. That reduction is exact and is the useful output.
attempt.obstruction: The volume |A_1(s) union A_2(t)| requires the joint distribution of the times at which a single moving grain sweeps two given sets, which for Brownian motion is the two-set Wiener sausage volume - a quantity with no closed form in any dimension. For ballistic motion it is a solid-angle computation and should be tractable, which suggests the inertial case of this problem is the one to do first.
attempt.key_identity: P(S_1 > s, S_2 > t) = exp(-lambda |A_1(s) union A_2(t)|) by the Poisson void probability, so the comparison probability is an explicit integral and the whole content is the volume of the union of two swept regions.

title: Detection of a ball before a fixed point in the inertial Boolean model
statement: For the inertial Boolean model, find the distribution of the detection time of a ball before a fixed point is hit.
status_search: Same search as E0103. Kept open.

attempt.method: Use the void-probability identity of E0104 with K_2 a single point, and see what the inertial geometry gives.
attempt.result: With K_2 = {x_0} a point, the set A_2(t) of grain initial conditions detecting x_0 by time t is, for ballistic grains of radius r and velocity law mu, the set of (y, v) with dist(x_0, y + [0,t] v) <= r, whose volume is c_d r^{d-1} t E[|v|] + O(r^d) - an exact computation, unlike the Brownian case. Hence P(the point is not hit by time t) = exp(-lambda c_d r^{d-1} E|v| t) exactly to leading order in r, i.e. the point-detection time is asymptotically EXPONENTIAL with an explicit rate. The joint law with the ball's detection time then follows from the same void probability applied to the union, and the conditional problem the source asks for reduces to computing the volume of the swept-region union for a ball and a point, which for ballistic motion is a solid-angle integral. So the inertial case is genuinely more tractable than the Brownian one, and this is the concrete reason to attack it first.
attempt.obstruction: The leading-order computation ignores the O(r^d) corrections and the correlation induced by grains that detect the ball and the point at nearby times; getting the exact distribution rather than the exponential asymptotics requires the full union volume, and the union of a spherical shell's sweep and a point's sweep has an overlap term that depends on the direction distribution.
attempt.key_identity: For ballistic grains, the set of initial conditions detecting a fixed point by time t has volume c_d r^{d-1} t E|v| + O(r^d), so point detection is asymptotically exponential with that explicit rate - a closed form the Brownian case does not have.

title: Stability of a spatial service system driven by the Brownian Boolean model
statement: Let Pi be an independent space-time Poisson process in R^d x R_+ of fixed intensity, whose points are interpreted as customers. The Brownian Boolean model is a space-time serving mechanism which clears points whenever it meets them. Find necessary and sufficient stability conditions. The source notes the connection to stability problems in queueing theory where the spatial dimension matters as much as the time dimension.
status_search: WebSearch 2026-09-08 on stability of spatial queueing systems served by moving servers and on the greedy/Poisson matching literature (Foss, Baccelli, Sankararaman). Related stability results exist for spatial birth-and-death and for the 'Poisson matching' models; the specific Boolean-model server was not found. Kept open.

attempt.method: Do the rate balance, which for a spatial system is a comparison of two densities rather than two rates.
attempt.result: Customers arrive at space-time intensity nu per unit volume per unit time. A single Brownian grain of radius r clears, in time t, a region of expected volume equal to the Wiener sausage volume: of order 2 pi t / log t in d = 2 and c_d r^{d-2} t in d >= 3. With grain intensity lambda the total clearing rate per unit volume is therefore lambda times that rate, so the necessary stability condition is nu < lambda c_d r^{d-2} for d >= 3, and nu < 2 pi lambda / log t for d = 2 - which DEGENERATES: in two dimensions the clearing rate per grain decays like 1/log t, so the naive balance says the system is unstable for every positive nu. That is the interesting content: the two-dimensional case is critical and stability, if it holds at all, must come from the grains' overlap structure rather than from a rate comparison. Recording that dichotomy (a genuine rate condition in d >= 3, a marginal case in d = 2, and total instability in d = 1 where the sausage volume is of order sqrt(t)) is the useful output.
attempt.obstruction: The rate balance is only necessary; sufficiency needs a Lyapunov function for a measure-valued process, and the natural candidate (total number of unserved customers in a window) is not Markov because the service depends on the whole past of the grain field. In d = 2 the logarithm means any Lyapunov argument must be run at a scale growing with time.
attempt.key_identity: A Brownian grain clears a Wiener-sausage volume of order c_d r^{d-2} t in d >= 3 but only 2 pi t / log t in d = 2 and of order sqrt(t) in d = 1, so a positive-rate stability condition exists only for d >= 3.

title: Existence and uniqueness of stationary measures for the local equation on sparse random graphs
statement: Can one establish general conditions for existence and uniqueness of stationary or invariant measures for the local equation - the autonomous reduced-dimension description of the marginal dynamics of an interacting particle system on a sparse random graph?
status_search: WebSearch 2026-09-08 on stationary measures of the local equation for interacting diffusions on sparse graphs (the Lacker-Ramanan-Wu programme). Existence and uniqueness results are known for specific models and for regular trees; a general theory was not found. Kept open.

attempt.method: Compare with the mean-field case, where existence and uniqueness for the nonlinear McKean-Vlasov equation is classical, and identify what the sparse case adds.
attempt.result: In the mean-field case the nonlinear equation's stationary measures are fixed points of a map on probability measures on the state space, and uniqueness follows from a contraction in Wasserstein distance under a smallness condition on the interaction. The local equation replaces that by a fixed-point problem on measures on PATH SPACE indexed by the root of a Galton-Watson tree, with the interaction entering through the conditional law of the neighbours' paths given the root's. So the contraction, if it exists, must be in a Wasserstein distance on path space with a weight that decays along the tree - and the natural smallness condition is that the interaction strength times the expected degree is less than one, which is exactly a subcriticality condition on the branching. That identifies the shape of a general theorem: uniqueness below a branching-type threshold, non-uniqueness (phase transition) above, matching the source's own Q2 about identifying phase transitions.
attempt.obstruction: The local equation is non-Markov in the root's state alone - it is a path-dependent equation involving conditional laws - so the fixed-point map acts on measures on C([0,T]) and the contraction constant involves the whole time horizon; a stationary theory needs the contraction to be uniform in T, which fails at any positive interaction strength unless the tree's degree is subcritical in a strong sense.
attempt.key_identity: The mean-field fixed point contracts when the interaction strength is small; on a sparse graph the analogue must contract along the tree, so the natural threshold is interaction strength times mean degree below one - a subcriticality rather than a smallness condition.

title: Large deviations for interacting particle systems on sparse random graphs
statement: Can one establish large deviation principles and concentration results for interacting particle systems on sparse random graphs? The source notes that such results are known for weakly interacting systems on complete and dense graphs.
status_search: WebSearch 2026-09-08 on large deviations for interacting diffusions on sparse graphs. The dense/mean-field theory (Dawson-Gartner and successors) is classical; sparse-graph large deviations were not found beyond special cases. Kept open.

attempt.method: Ask what the rate function would be a functional of, since that determines whether a Dawson-Gartner argument can be adapted.
attempt.result: In the mean-field case the empirical measure is a sufficient statistic and the rate function is a relative entropy on path space. On a sparse graph the empirical measure loses the graph structure and the correct object is the empirical distribution of ROOTED NEIGHBOURHOOD-DECORATED paths, i.e. a measure on the space of rooted marked graphs - and the natural rate function is the relative entropy of that unimodular measure with respect to the product of the local equation's law, corrected by an edge term. The edge correction is forced by unimodularity: any candidate rate function must vanish on unimodular measures consistent with the graph's local limit, so it is an entropy relative to the local limit minus an edge entropy - exactly the structure of the Bordenave-Caputo large deviation rate for the empirical neighbourhood distribution of sparse graphs. That identification says the machinery to adapt is Bordenave-Caputo rather than Dawson-Gartner.
attempt.obstruction: Bordenave-Caputo's rate function is for the STATIC neighbourhood distribution and is proved for specific graph ensembles; adding the dynamics multiplies the state space by path space, and the resulting entropy is not lower semicontinuous in the local topology without a tightness input that the unbounded path space does not supply.
attempt.key_identity: On a sparse graph the sufficient statistic is the empirical distribution of rooted neighbourhood-decorated paths, so the rate function must be an entropy relative to the local limit minus an edge term - the Bordenave-Caputo structure, not the Dawson-Gartner one.

title: Limit theorems for Nash equilibria of games on sparse interaction networks
statement: Can one establish limit theorems for Nash equilibria of games with a large number of agents in which the interaction network of agents is sparse rather than the complete graph? The source notes that recent work covers networks with diverging degrees, and that there are only a few works on graphs with uniformly bounded degree.
status_search: WebSearch 2026-09-08 on graphon games and mean-field games on sparse graphs. The graphon-game literature covers dense networks; sparse (bounded-degree) mean-field games are treated in a few papers (Lacker-Soret and others) for specific structures. Kept open.

attempt.method: Ask what breaks when the degree stays bounded, by comparing with the graphon case.
attempt.result: In the dense case each agent's payoff depends on an average over a diverging number of neighbours, so a law of large numbers applies and the equilibrium condition becomes a fixed point against a deterministic aggregate - the mean-field game. With bounded degree the neighbour average does not concentrate, so the equilibrium condition is a fixed point against a RANDOM aggregate, and the resulting object is not a mean-field game but a game on a Galton-Watson tree with a consistency (unimodularity) constraint. The immediate structural consequence is that equilibrium uniqueness cannot be expected in general: games on trees typically have multiple equilibria above a branching threshold, exactly as spin systems on trees have multiple Gibbs measures, so the right limit theorem is a statement about the SET of equilibria and its dependence on a reconstruction-type threshold. Framing the question that way, rather than as a convergence-to-a-unique-equilibrium statement, is the useful step.
attempt.obstruction: Fixed points on trees are computed by belief propagation, which converges only below the reconstruction threshold; above it, selecting the equilibrium that is the limit of the finite-graph equilibria requires a Gibbs-measure-selection argument, and no such selection principle exists for games, where there is no free energy to extremise.
attempt.key_identity: With bounded degree the neighbour average does not concentrate, so the limit is a game on a Galton-Watson tree with a unimodularity constraint; multiplicity of equilibria above a reconstruction-type threshold is then the expected phenomenon, as for Gibbs measures on trees.

title: Dimension-linear relaxation time for generalized reflected Brownian motion
statement: Under the assumptions of Theorem 1.3, the generalized reflected Brownian motion GRBM(R, mu, Sigma, U) is uniformly exponentially ergodic with exponent of order 1/d: there exist W : R^d -> [1, infinity) and C > 0 such that ||P^t(x, .) - pi(.)||_{TV} <= W(x) exp(-C t / d). This would mean the relaxation time to global equilibrium is of order d for a class of GRBMs.
status_search: WebSearch 2026-09-08 on dimension dependence of the relaxation time of reflected Brownian motion in a cone or orthant and on the O'Connell-Yor process. The source's own Theorem 1.3 gives exponential ergodicity without an explicit dimension dependence; I found no proof of the 1/d rate. Kept open.

attempt.method: Test the conjectured 1/d against the one case where the answer is computable, the free (unreflected) case with a confining drift, and against the geometry of the orthant.
attempt.result: For a d-dimensional Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process the relaxation time is the inverse of the smallest drift eigenvalue and is dimension-free, so a 1/d rate must come from the reflection, not the drift. The natural mechanism is that equilibration requires each of the d faces to be visited, and the process visits faces one at a time, so the relaxation time should be the time to visit all faces - a coupon-collector-type quantity of order d log d rather than d, unless the visits are simultaneous. That is a concrete tension with the conjecture: the coupon-collector heuristic predicts d log d, and the conjecture asserts d. Either the faces equilibrate in parallel (which the Lyapunov function would have to show) or the conjectured rate is off by a logarithm. Flagging that discrepancy is the honest output; I have not settled which is right, and the source's Theorem 1.3 does not decide it.
attempt.obstruction: Resolving the discrepancy needs a lower bound on the relaxation time, and lower bounds for reflected diffusions in the orthant require a test function concentrated near one face whose expected decay is slow - which for a GRBM depends on the reflection matrix R, so the answer may be R-dependent and neither d nor d log d in general.
attempt.key_identity: An Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process has dimension-free relaxation, so any d-dependence comes from the reflection; visiting all d faces is a coupon-collector-type event suggesting d log d rather than the conjectured d.

title: Free energy fluctuations of the Sherrington-Kirkpatrick model at the critical temperature
statement: For the Sherrington-Kirkpatrick model at the critical value beta_c = 1, Var(F_N^{SK}(beta_c)) = (1/6) N^{-2} log N + O(N^{-2}) as N tends to infinity. The survey records as the best available progress the result of Chen and Lam giving Var(F_N(beta_c)) <= C(N^{-2}(log N)^2 + 1) and a companion statement.
status_search: WebSearch 2026-09-08 covered by the survey itself (fetched 2025-11 version), which states the conjecture and the state of the art. The bound available carries (log N)^2 where the conjecture has log N, and no matching lower bound of that order was reported. Kept open.

attempt.method: Locate the source of the log N by comparing with the two neighbouring regimes whose answers are known.
attempt.result: Above criticality the free energy fluctuation is of order N^{-1} with a Gaussian limit (Aizenman-Lebowitz-Ruelle), giving variance of order N^{-2} with no logarithm; the log N at beta_c must therefore come from the divergence of the high-temperature variance formula as beta approaches 1. In the ALR formula the variance is a series whose terms behave like beta^{2k}/(2k), so at beta = 1 the series is the harmonic series and diverges logarithmically - and truncating it at the scale where the finite-N corrections cut it off, namely k of order log N, produces exactly (1/2) times the sum of 1/(2k) up to log N, i.e. a coefficient of the form (1/4) log log N or (1/6) log N depending on the cutoff scale. The conjectured constant 1/6 therefore encodes the precise cutoff, and testing which cutoff gives 1/6 is a concrete check on the conjecture. This is a heuristic reconstruction of where the constant comes from; it is not a derivation of it.
attempt.obstruction: The truncation scale is set by the breakdown of the high-temperature expansion at beta = 1, which is exactly where the replica-symmetric solution becomes unstable; controlling it needs a uniform expansion through the critical window, and the available Chen-Lam bound loses a logarithm precisely there.
attempt.key_identity: The Aizenman-Lebowitz-Ruelle variance is a series in beta^{2k}/(2k) which becomes harmonic at beta_c = 1; the conjectured log N is the harmonic sum cut off at a scale set by N, and the constant 1/6 encodes that cutoff.

title: Weak and strong disorder critical temperatures for directed Brownian polymers in a Poissonian environment
statement: For the directed Brownian polymer in a Poissonian environment, define the critical inverse temperatures beta_c^{+,dir} = sup{beta >= 0 : lim_t P[(W_t^{dir,beta})^{1/2}] > 0} and beta_c^{-,dir} = inf{beta >= 0 : lim_t P[(W_t^{dir,beta})^{1/2}] > 0}, the analogues of the weak/strong disorder transition. The survey formulates conjectures about these critical points for the directed model.
status_search: WebSearch 2026-09-08 on weak and strong disorder for Brownian directed polymers in a Poissonian environment (Comets-Yoshida, Comets-Cosco). The existence of a single critical point and its coincidence with the L^1-L^2 threshold in high dimension is known in several lattice settings; the Poissonian Brownian version was not found resolved. Kept open.

attempt.method: Ask whether the two critical points can differ, since the conjecture is essentially that they coincide.
attempt.result: The normalised partition function W_t is a positive martingale, so its limit is either almost surely zero or has positive expectation, and the set of beta for which the limit is positive is an interval containing 0 by a standard monotonicity (Comets-Yoshida) argument. Hence beta_c^+ = beta_c^- automatically whenever that monotonicity holds - the two definitions bracket the same number and the conjecture reduces to establishing monotonicity of the weak-disorder property in beta for the Poissonian Brownian model. Monotonicity in beta is proved on the lattice by a size-biasing/coupling argument that uses the discreteness of the environment; the Poissonian environment is continuous, and whether the same coupling exists is the actual content. Reducing the conjecture to a monotonicity statement is the useful step.
attempt.obstruction: The lattice proof couples environments at two temperatures through a monotone rearrangement of i.i.d. weights; for a Poisson field the analogous coupling would have to thin the point process in a way that preserves the polymer measure's normalisation, and thinning changes the intensity rather than the temperature, so the coupling is not immediate.
attempt.key_identity: W_t is a positive martingale, so weak disorder is a zero-one property, and the upper and lower critical temperatures coincide as soon as weak disorder is monotone in beta - which is what a coupling in the Poissonian environment would have to supply.

title: KPZ fluctuations for the free energy of the Brownian polymer in strong disorder
statement: For all nonzero beta, nu and r, there exists a constant sigma(beta, nu) such that (log Z_t - p(beta,nu) t) / (sigma(beta,nu) t^{1/3}) converges in law to the Tracy-Widom GOE distribution as t tends to infinity, in contrast with the weak disorder regime where the polymer is diffusive.
status_search: WebSearch 2026-09-08 on KPZ fluctuations for Brownian polymers in a Poissonian environment. The KPZ exponent and Tracy-Widom limits are proved for exactly solvable models (O'Connell-Yor, the semi-discrete polymer, the stochastic heat equation); the Poissonian Brownian polymer of the survey is not known to be integrable and no such result was found. Kept open.

attempt.method: Ask what integrability the known Tracy-Widom proofs use, and whether the Poissonian model has any of it.
attempt.result: Every proof of a Tracy-Widom limit for a positive-temperature polymer goes through an exact formula: a Whittaker measure (O'Connell-Yor), a Macdonald process (log-gamma), or the replica/Bethe-ansatz moment formula for the stochastic heat equation. The Poissonian Brownian polymer has a distinguishing feature that is worth stating: its environment is a Poisson field, so the moments of Z_t are given by an exponential functional of a Poisson process, and the k-th moment satisfies a closed evolution equation with a pairwise interaction of delta type - the same structure as the replica equation for the stochastic heat equation, but with a jump kernel rather than a delta. So the model is a candidate for the replica route, and the obstacle is that the moments grow too fast (like exp(c k^3) or faster for a Poisson environment) for the moment problem to be determinate. That identification - moments computable but not determinate - is the concrete state of play and explains why the conjecture is stated rather than proved.
attempt.obstruction: For a Poisson environment the exponential moments of the environment are doubly exponential in beta, so E[Z_t^k] grows fast enough that the moment problem is indeterminate and no Carleman-type argument recovers the law. The replica method is therefore formal here, unlike for the Gaussian stochastic heat equation where the k-th moment grows like exp(c k^3 t) and the same indeterminacy is handled by an analytic continuation that has no Poissonian analogue.
attempt.key_identity: The moments of the Poissonian polymer partition function solve a closed delta-type replica system, as for the stochastic heat equation, but grow doubly exponentially in the temperature, so the moment problem is indeterminate and the replica route is formal.
